name: FontGen
tagline: Web tool for generating custom fonts and downloadable typefaces without opening a type design app.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Turning a set of glyph images into an installable TTF is a solved, well documented pipeline: trace bitmaps to vectors, drop the contours into a font table, write the file. An agent can absolutely stand that up locally in a weekend, and the output will install and render in your OS and browser. What it will not do is make the font good: spacing, kerning pairs, consistent stroke weight, diacritics, hinting at small sizes, and anything beyond basic Latin are all grind work that a one-shot skips entirely. If you want one personal handwriting font for a signature or a header, build it. If you want something you would ship to clients, the boring type craft is the actual product.
coreLoopDIY: Takes scanned or drawn glyph images, traces them to vector outlines, and compiles a working TTF/WOFF2 you can install and use in CSS.
requirements: A scanned glyph sheet or 60+ individual glyph PNGs, one per character
Comfort installing a font on your own machine to test it
whatYouLose: Automatic spacing and kerning that does not look drunk
Glyph coverage beyond basic Latin: accents, currency, math, punctuation edge cases
Hinting and rendering QA across Windows, macOS, and small sizes
A hosted preview and share flow, plus webfont delivery
Any curated template or style library to start from instead of a blank sheet
moatNotes: The moat here is typographic taste and glyph libraries, not code. The file format is public and the tooling is free.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a font that is technically valid and a font that looks right are different artifacts, and the gap between them is hundreds of small spacing decisions. A paid generator has already made most of those decisions for you, ships with coverage you did not think to ask for, and hands you a file that renders cleanly instead of one you have to debug in three browsers. For a one-off personal font the DIY route is fine. For anything with a deadline attached, paying beats learning what side bearings are.
notes: The file writing is the easy half. The half that decides whether your font looks amateur is spacing, and no agent will do that for you.
prompt:
Build a local font generator called glyphforge. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Python 3.11, FastAPI, uvicorn, single HTML page with vanilla JS and no build step
- Pillow for image handling, potracer for bitmap to vector tracing, fontTools for font assembly
- Everything runs on localhost, all files stay on disk

Core pipeline:
1. Input: a folder of PNG or JPG images named by unicode char, e.g. A.png, a.png, ampersand.png. Also accept a single scanned grid sheet plus a JSON layout file that maps grid cells to characters, and slice it.
2. Preprocess each glyph: grayscale, Otsu threshold, deskew, crop to ink bounds, normalize height against a configured cap height and x-height.
3. Trace to closed contours with potracer, simplify, then build glyphs with fontTools.pens.ttGlyphPen.TTGlyphPen on a 1000 unit em.
4. Set advance width per glyph as ink width plus a configurable side bearing, written to hmtx.
5. Assemble a real font with fontTools.fontBuilder: head, hhea, hmtx, cmap, name, OS/2, post. Export both TTF and WOFF2.
6. Optional naive kerning: a GPOS pair kerning table generated from a simple outline-proximity heuristic, off by default behind a flag.

Web UI, one page:
- Drag a folder or grid sheet in, see every traced glyph as inline SVG
- Sliders for side bearing, cap height, x-height, stroke threshold, with live retrace
- A live text preview that loads the generated WOFF2 via a blob URL and @font-face
- Download buttons for TTF and WOFF2, plus a CSS snippet

Explicitly out of scope: hinting, variable font axes, OpenType features beyond basic kerning, non-Latin scripts, automatic diacritic composition. Say so in the README.

Also ship: a CLI entry point (python -m glyphforge build ./glyphs --name "My Hand") that does the same thing headlessly, a tests folder with a sample 5 glyph fixture asserting the output parses in fontTools and has a valid cmap, and a README that tells me how to install the font on macOS, Windows, and Linux.

No secrets needed. If you add any config, use a .env file and commit a .env.example.
